notes:
I've written these notes from the pages I could actually read. Each point is in my own words and ends with its URL. One gap to flag first: I didn't get to read newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, any Pentecostal or Lutheran site, or anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. So the "other views" below are limited. Catholic and Church Fathers material appears only where Protestant reference sites quote it.

---

## Luke 10:1–21: Research notes

**v. 1: Seventy or seventy-two, and why pairs**
- **Traditional reading:** This was a larger group of followers beyond the Twelve. Guzik (Enduring Word) suggests the number may echo the seventy elders with Moses, the Sanhedrin, or the seventy translators of the Septuagint. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Why two by two:** Clarke, quoted by Guzik, gives three reasons: to teach agreement among ministers, so that two witnesses confirm every matter, and so they could comfort each other. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **The manuscript question:** Ellicott says some MSS. of importance give "seventy-two," but the evidence preponderates in favour of the reading "seventy." https://biblehub.com/luke/10-1.htm. Precept Austin calls it one of the most difficult textual questions in the New Testament to resolve, since the evidence is quite evenly distributed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-10-commentary. Utley (bible.org) lists the manuscripts on each side. He says that if the more unusual reading is likely original, "seventy-two" wins. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307
- **What the number symbolises:** The Bible Hub study notes link seventy-two to the list of nations in Genesis 10, hinting at a worldwide mission. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-1.htm. Utley agrees this fits Luke's purpose (cf. Luke 24:47). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307. Pett argues the other way. Because they went in pairs, he thinks the number does not stand for the world's nations. He reads it as Moses' elders, pointing to a "new Israel." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-10.html
- **Their role:** They were forerunners, not substitutes for Christ. Their job was to inform people about Him and stir up longing for His coming (Preacher's Homiletical Commentary). https://studylight.org/commentaries/phc/luke-10.html
- **Church Fathers (via the Pulpit Commentary):** The Fathers dwell on the sacred symbolism of the desert-wanderings especially mentioned at Elim—"twelve wells and seventy palm trees," which they read as the Twelve and the Seventy. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-10.html
- **Modern scholarship (via Coffman):** Coffman reports that scholars such as Easton, Klostermann and Creed denied that this mission happened, because the instructions are so like those given to the Twelve. Coffman himself rejects their view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-10.html

**v. 2: The harvest and the prayer**
- **Traditional reading:** Jesus saw great human need as an opportunity. The verse teaches the need for prayer, workers and God's call, and that the harvest belongs to Him (Guzik). Spurgeon notes that the Greek word for "send out" is the one used for casting out a demon, so it takes God's power to "drive" workers out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **A caution:** Utley says we are told to pray for God to send workers, not simply to go ourselves. "Need does not constitute a call," he writes. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307
- **Prayer and answer:** The Homiletical Commentary says we pray this whenever we say "Thy kingdom come." Sending the seventy was itself an answer to the prayer Jesus had urged earlier. https://studylight.org/commentaries/phc/luke-10.html

**v. 3: Lambs among wolves**
- **Traditional reading:** Jesus was sent the same way, as a lamb (Guzik). Spurgeon adds a hopeful note: sheep far outnumber wolves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Other notes:** The "I" in "I am sending you" is emphatic. Their confidence was to rest in the One who sent them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/phc/luke-10.html. Utley sees here a foreshadowing of how Jesus would be received in Jerusalem. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307

**v. 4: No purse, bag or sandals; greet no one**
- **Traditional reading:** They were not to be distracted by material concerns or by long rounds of etiquette (Guzik, quoting Morrison on how drawn-out Eastern greetings were). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **The point:** They were to depend totally on God's provision. The greetings meant long ceremonial rituals, and the mission was too urgent for delay (cf. 2 Kings 4:29) (Utley). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307

**vv. 5–6: "Peace to this house" and the "man of peace"**
- **"Son of peace":** Clarke, quoted by Guzik, says the Hebrew idiom means a peaceable man who also has a good reputation. Inns of the day were often unsuitable places for the messengers to stay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **More than a greeting:** A bible.org piece quoted by Precept Austin says the greeting was an actual announcement of God's blessing if the people accepted and submitted to the message of God's kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-10-commentary
- **Catholic scholarship (via Utley):** The *Jerome Biblical Commentary* takes the phrase to mean that salvation has come to the welcoming home. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307
- **Church Fathers (via Aquinas' *Golden Chain*, Spanish text on StudyLight):** Chrysostom calls peace the mother of all good things. That is why the greeting comes first. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-7.html

**v. 7: Stay in one house; the worker deserves his wages**
- **Traditional reading:** The support they received was proper pay, not charity (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/. Gill puts it strongly: your diet is a debt, and not a gratuity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-7.html
- **A guard against greed:** Barclay mentions early rules for travelling prophets. A prophet who stayed too long, or asked for money, was to be counted false. The labourer is worthy of his hire, but the servant of a crucified Master cannot be a seeker for luxury. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-7.html
- **Link to Paul:** Ellicott finds it striking that Paul quotes these exact words as "Scripture" in 1 Timothy 5:18. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-7.htm
- **Catholic (Lapide, Spanish text on StudyLight):** He takes the "wages" to mean food and keep, not money, because preaching the kingdom has no price. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-7.html

**v. 8: Eat what is set before you**
- Utley says the mission mattered more than food laws (Mark 7; Acts 10). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307
- Coffman says the area was largely Gentile (Trans-Jordan), so the messengers should not burden hosts by asking for kosher food. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-10.html

**v. 9: Heal the sick; "the kingdom of God is near you"**
- **Traditional reading:** The healings showed the kingdom coming with power, shown in acts of mercy. The Greek *engiken* can mean either "has arrived" or "has drawn near" (Guzik, citing Pate). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Where Protestants differ:** Utley says the verse is controversial because some hold that the kingdom is only future. He argues instead that the kingdom began with Jesus and will be completed at His return. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307
- **Who was to be healed:** Utley gives two possible readings: everyone, to confirm the message, or only those who had faith. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307

**vv. 10–12: Wiping off the dust; "more bearable for Sodom"**
- **Traditional reading:** The towns had to know the price of rejecting Jesus. Guzik adds a challenge: many Christians today could not honestly say to those who reject them that the kingdom had come near. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Background:** Shaking off dust echoes Nehemiah 5:13, a sign of serious warning. https://biblehub.com/luke/10.htm
- **Degrees of judgment:** Both Utley and Guzik take v. 12 to teach that punishment will differ by degree. Utley also warns against building whole systems from one text, or turning details into a "Christian Talmud." https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307

**vv. 13–15: Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum**
- **Traditional reading:** More light brings more accountability. Capernaum was "exalted" because it was Jesus' home base. Chorazin is a reminder that the Gospels are sketches, not full biographies (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Notes from Utley:** "Woe" is a prophetic funeral cry. No ministry in Chorazin is recorded. Tyre and Sidon were symbols of pride. The question in v. 15 expects the answer "no." https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307
- **Hades:** Utley mentions the rabbinic idea of a two-part Hades and offers a view on what happened at Jesus' resurrection. This is his own position and is debated. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21307

**v. 16: Hearing you is hearing Me**
- The messengers were Jesus' representatives. They should not hold either praise or rejection too tightly (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/. Rejecting the messengers is akin to rejecting Christ Himself. https://biblehub.com/luke/10.htm

**v. 17: "Even the demons submit to us"**
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott hears a joyful surprise. They had not looked for such great and immediate results. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-17.htm
- **An unexpected blessing:** Guzik notes that the seventy were never told to cast out demons. Spurgeon: not one lamb was eaten by the wolves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Background (Keener, via Light of Israel):** Exorcists usually used long incantations, so the disciples were amazed that Jesus' name worked at once. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/luke-10.html

**v. 18: "I saw Satan fall like lightning"** (interpretations differ widely)
- **The original fall before creation:** GotQuestions links it to Isaiah 14:12 and says it speaks of Jesus' pre-existence and the Lord's victory over the power of Satan in a general sense. https://www.gotquestions.org/Satan-fall-like-lightning.html. Gill takes the same line. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/luke/10-18.html
- **The present defeat:** Ellicott says the verb means Jesus "was beholding" the fall as it happened. The main sense is that Satan was being thrown from his usurped rule. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-18.htm
- **A prophecy:** The Pulpit Commentary calls the words prophetic rather than descriptive, foreseeing the gospel's victory over paganism. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-18.htm
- **John Calvin:** The thunder of the Gospel makes Satan fall like lightning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-18.html
- **Speed, not place:** Barnes reads "from heaven" as describing the lightning, so the point is how fast Satan fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/10-18.htm
- **Church Fathers (reported on Bible Hub):** The Fathers took it as the fall of the angels at the beginning. They read it as a warning to the disciples against pride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/10-18.htm
- **A future event:** Light of Israel links it to Revelation 12. Constable instead thinks Isaiah 14 is about a human king, and that Jesus means a present humbling of Satan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-18.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET note):** Probably an allusion to Isaiah 14:12. The exorcisms picture Satan's greater defeat. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Luk&chapter=10&verse=18

**v. 19: Treading on snakes and scorpions**
- **Literal or figurative:** Bible Hub's notes say the promise can be literal, as when Paul shook off the viper in Acts 28. But it is not a dare to court danger. "Nothing will harm you" means final safety, even if believers are martyred. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-19.htm
- **Clarke:** He reads it as complete victory, drawing on the ancient custom of trampling defeated kings. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/luke/10-19.html
- **Other views:** I found no Pentecostal, word-of-faith or prosperity treatment of this verse on the permitted sites.

**v. 20: Rejoice that your names are written in heaven**
- **Traditional reading:** Casting out demons does limited good in this life. A name written in heaven is an eternal blessing (GotQuestions). https://www.gotquestions.org/Satan-fall-like-lightning.html
- **Contrast with Satan:** Bible Hub sets the disciples' secure heavenly citizenship against Satan's permanent exile. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-18.htm. Pett says what truly matters is not these passing achievements. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-10.html

**v. 21: Hidden from the wise, revealed to little children** (here the traditions clearly differ)
- **Reformed / Calvinist:** John Piper sees here the free, electing love of God. His point is not that certain classes are chosen, but that God is free to choose the least likely people. https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/what-makes-jesus-rejoice. Fortner likewise stresses God's absolute sovereignty in showing saving mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-21.html
- **Arminian / Restoration Movement (as StudyLight labels Coffman):** God did not hide the truth on a whim. Both groups received the same revelation. Those who kept rejecting it lost it and were confirmed in their blindness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/10-21.html
- **Middle readings:** Clarke, citing Bishop Pearce, says the thanks are for the revealing, not the hiding. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/luke/10-21.html. Benson says God "suffered" the truth to be hidden from the proud. Jesus rejoiced in grace shown, not in anyone's ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/10-21.htm. Burkitt speaks of judicial blinding of those who first shut their own eyes. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/10-21.htm
- **Jesus' joy:** This is a rare moment of joy in His life. Spurgeon says Jesus was content with the kind of converts and preachers the Father had given Him. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/10-21.htm
- **Not anti-learning:** Bible Hub's notes say the verse confronts pride, not the use of the mind. It parallels Isaiah 29:14 and 1 Corinthians 1. https://biblehub.com/luke/10-21.htm

---

**Gaps to fill if you need them:** Lutheran, Pentecostal and charismatic, and Orthodox readings (especially of vv. 17–19), and anything on prosperity or word-of-faith uses of v. 19. Another round of searching on lcms.org, 1517.org, pneumareview.com, samstorms.org, oca.org and newadvent.org (Aquinas' *Catena Aurea* on Luke 10) would be the next step.
